title: FRM Foundations, Lesson 10: RAROC and economic capital - the price of risk measured in capital
subtitle: Why a desk earning 100bn can be destroying value while a desk earning 40bn is not
whyItMatters: Every bank has several businesses asking for more capital at the same time, and absolute profit cannot settle which of them deserves it. RAROC is the common language that lets a bond desk be compared with a retail lending book, and it is why risk management has a seat at the capital allocation table rather than only a control function behind it.
openingQuestion: Desk A earns 100bn on 1,000bn of economic capital. Desk B earns 40bn on 250bn of economic capital. The bank's cost of capital is 12%. Which desk is creating value?
openingOptions: Desk A, because its absolute profit is two and a half times larger than B's
Desk B, whose RAROC of 16% clears the hurdle while desk A returns only 10%
Both equally, since they sit in one bank and share the same cost of capital
It cannot be settled without knowing the revenue each desk generated
explanation: RAROC divides risk-adjusted profit by economic capital: desk A returns 100/1,000 = 10%, desk B returns 40/250 = 16%. The 12% cost of capital is the line that decides. Desk A earns a large number but absorbs so much capital that the profit does not cover what shareholders demand for it - roughly 20bn of value destroyed every year. Desk B is smaller, but every unit of capital it holds earns above the hurdle. This is exactly why absolute profit is the wrong measure when capital is being allocated.

diagram.label: Divided by economic capital - capital for UNexpected loss
Compared with the hurdle rate shareholders demand
Above the hurdle creates value, below it destroys value

realWorldExample.description: Before 2008, many banks measured their trading desks by absolute profit and paid bonuses off that number. Desks found ways to earn steadily by taking on risks that hardly ever materialise but are severe when they do - selling insurance against the tail. The profit looked good year after year because the economic capital for that tail never entered the denominator. When the tail arrived, the loss dwarfed every year of accumulated profit.

quiz.question: Scenario: a business earns 60bn of profit, has 10bn of expected loss and 400bn of economic capital. What is its RAROC?
options: 17.5% (= (60 + 10) ÷ 400, adding the expected loss by mistake)
15% (= 60 ÷ 400, forgetting to deduct the expected loss)
12.5% (= (60 − 10) ÷ 400, deducting EL before dividing)
6% (= (60 − 10) ÷ 400 × 0.48, one multiplication too many)
quiz.explanation: The numerator of RAROC is profit net of expected loss, because EL is an ordinary cost of doing business rather than a surprise: (60 − 10) ÷ 400 = 12.5%. Forgetting to deduct it flatters precisely the riskiest businesses, because that is where expected loss is largest.

quiz.question: Economic capital is sized to absorb which kind of loss?
options: Only the portion of losses that arises from operational risk events
Expected loss, the average amount that can be computed each year
Every loss that could conceivably occur, with no exception at all
Unexpected loss, the part that runs beyond the average
quiz.explanation: Expected loss is already covered by provisions and already priced into the product. Capital exists for the part that runs beyond the average - the part that cannot be priced in, because nobody knows when it arrives. Sizing capital to cover every conceivable loss would mean holding capital against a number with no upper bound, which is why a confidence level has to be chosen. And economic capital spans credit, market and operational risk together rather than one of them alone. Confusing expected with unexpected loss is the most common conceptual error in reading a capital report.

quiz.question: Why does using absolute profit to allocate capital create the wrong incentive?
options: Because it rewards whichever business takes the most risk
Because it always favours businesses with lower revenue
Because it cannot be computed for a newly opened business line
Because it ignores the staff costs carried by each business
quiz.explanation: High risk usually comes with high nominal profit. If profit is the only thing measured, the business carrying the most risk wins the competition for capital every time, even when each unit of capital it holds earns less than it should. RAROC puts risk into the denominator, so the reward only arrives when profit clears the price of the risk taken. Absolute profit does subtract staff costs and can be computed for a new desk, so neither of those is the defect - the defect is that it is silent about what was risked to produce the number.

quiz.question: Scenario: a business has a RAROC of 9% while the bank's cost of capital is 12%. What is the correct conclusion?
options: It is creating value, because its RAROC is still positive
It is destroying value even though it reports a profit
It is breaking even, neither creating nor destroying value
No comparison is possible, since the two are in different units
quiz.explanation: Being profitable and creating value are two different things. Shareholders demand 12% on the capital they leave in the business; this one returns 9%, so every unit of capital parked there makes the bank 3% a year poorer than simply returning it. The income statement never shows that gap, because the cost of equity is not an accounting expense. Both figures are annual returns on capital, so they are in the same units and directly comparable - that comparability is the whole reason RAROC is expressed as a ratio.

quiz.question: What is the biggest weakness of RAROC when it is used to compare two businesses?
options: RAROC always produces a higher figure for a long-established business
RAROC cannot be applied to any business that takes collateral
Economic capital is a modelled number, so only one method compares
RAROC cannot be computed unless the bank's shares are listed
quiz.explanation: The denominator is a modelled number rather than an observed one. Two businesses using different confidence levels, or different correlation assumptions, produce economic capital figures that are not comparable, and a RAROC league table built on them reflects modelling choices more than business performance. Nothing about RAROC depends on a listing - the cost of capital can be estimated for a private bank - and it applies perfectly well to secured lending, where collateral simply lowers the loss given default that feeds the model.

practicePrompt.question: Business A earns 200bn on 2,500bn of economic capital with 50bn of expected loss. Business B earns 90bn on 600bn of economic capital with 15bn of expected loss. The cost of capital is 12%. Where should new capital go?
options: Business B, with a RAROC of 12.5% against 6% for business A
Business A, because its absolute profit is more than twice as large
Both, since each of them clears the 12% cost of capital hurdle
It cannot be decided without knowing the revenue of each business
practicePrompt.explanation: A's RAROC is (200 − 50)/2,500 = 6%; B's is (90 − 15)/600 = 12.5%. With a 12% cost of capital, A is DESTROYING value despite earning 200bn, and B is creating it despite earning less than half as much. That is the entire reason RAROC exists: absolute profit always rewards the business taking the most risk, because taking more risk almost always produces more nominal profit. One caveat: the denominator is a modelled figure, so comparing RAROC across two businesses only means something when the economic capital of both is computed on the same method.

keyTakeaways: RAROC = (Profit − Expected loss) ÷ Economic capital, compared with the cost of capital to see whether the business creates or destroys value
Economic capital carries UNexpected loss; expected loss already sits in provisions and in the price of the product
Absolute profit always rewards the business taking the most risk, so it is the wrong measure for allocating capital
The denominator is a modelled number, so comparing RAROC across businesses only means something on a single method

summary.keyIdea: RAROC turns risk into a cost denominated in money, which is what finally lets every business be weighed on the same scale. It is also the point where risk management stops being the brake and starts taking part in deciding where capital goes.

application.message: When you read a bank's segment report, do not stop at the profit line. Ask what share of capital that segment absorbs, and whether the profit clears the bank's own cost of capital.

sections.text: Two trading desks are both asking for more capital. One earned 100bn last year, the other earned 40bn. With only those two numbers, the decision looks obvious - and it is almost always wrong.
Risk is a cost, and capital is the invoice

A bank has to hold capital in proportion to the risk of each activity, enough to absorb the losses that run beyond the average. That capital is not free: shareholders leave the money in and demand a return on it. So a business that consumes a lot of capital is carrying a real cost - it is just a cost that never appears on the income statement.
The three pieces of the formula

The numerator is profit net of expected loss, because the average loss is a known cost of doing business and is already priced in. The denominator is economic capital, the amount needed to survive unexpected loss at a chosen confidence level. The result is compared with the cost of capital: above it creates value, below it destroys value.

The denominator comes from a model, not from observation. Lowering the confidence level, or assuming risks are less correlated than they are, lowers economic capital, and RAROC improves without anything changing in the business. This is why the capital methodology has to be set centrally and validated independently, rather than left to each business to choose.

sections.label: Worth remembering
sections.text: A desk with an unusually high and unusually stable RAROC over many years deserves suspicion more than praise: it is usually a sign of tail risk that never made it into the denominator, rather than of a durable advantage.
